sentences.text: The name Camptosaurus translates to 'flexible lizard', a title derived from Greek words meaning 'bent' and 'lizard'.
This dinosaur was a heavily built herbivore featuring robust hindlimbs and broad feet equipped with four toes.
Typical adults measured between 5 and 6 meters in length and weighed from 500 to 1000 kilograms.
However, the largest known fragments suggest that some individuals could reach approximately 6.79 meters in length.
Later strata indicate that adult specimens averaged more than 7.9 meters in length and stood over 2 meters tall.
Its teeth were packed more tightly in the jaw than those of other euornithopods found in the Morrison Formation.
A fossilized embryo roughly 23 centimeters long attributed to Camptosaurus was recovered from the Morrison Formation at the Dinosaur National Monument in Utah.
Remains of a small euornithopod were discovered by William Harlow Reed in Albany County, Wyoming, on September 4, 1879.
That same year, Professor Othniel Charles Marsh initially described and named the find as Camptonotus, or 'flexible spine'.
Marsh later renamed the genus Camptosaurus in 1885 because the original name Camptonotus was already used for a cricket.
He named the type species C. dispar in 1879 based on fossils from Quarry 13 near Como Bluff, Wyoming, and named C. amplus based on a foot found by Arthur Lakes at Quarry 1A.
There are currently 42 recorded fossil occurrences of the genus Camptosaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
Extensive wear on Camptosaurus teeth indicates a diet of relatively tough vegetation.
Scientists believe Camptosaurus could reach speeds of 25 km/h based on studies of other iguanodontians.
Camptosaurus lived alongside theropods like Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus, sauropods like Apatosaurus and Diplodocus, and ornithischians like Dryosaurus and Stegosaurus in the Morrison Formation.
The only theropod found in the deepest layers of the quarry was the relatively small Coelurus, which posed no threat to adult Camptosaurus.
Marsh assigned Camptosaurus to its own family, Camptosauridae, in 1885.
Some authors also consider it a member of the family Iguanodontidae, but this is a matter of debate.
The parent group of the genus Camptosaurus is Ankylopollexia.
Camptosaurus lived during the late Jurassic period, approximately between 160 and 145 million years ago, from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages.
Specimens of C. dispar from Quarry 13 date to the Callovian-Oxfordian stages of the Late Jurassic.
Camptosaurus lived in what is now western North America.
Three species of Camptosaurus were found in the Morrison Formation across the US states of Colorado, Oklahoma, Utah, and Wyoming.
It is debated whether C. prestwichii belongs in Camptosaurus; some researchers argue it should remain in the separate genus Cumnoria as it is more closely related to advanced iguanodonts.
An analysis suggests C. aphanoecetes is more closely related to advanced iguanodonts, leading to its reclassification as Uteodon.
Krumenacker et al. (2026) described three iguanodontian specimens from the Simon Quarry in Wyoming that have a morphology distinct from Dryosaurus and Camptosaurus.
